amendments.rule: The definite direct-object marker `אֵת` (H853) has no English realization of its own and is normally its own `unrepresented` unit; that is the ruling on the large majority of its occurrences. It takes English only where the ASV spends a word on the object relation itself and no other morpheme licenses that word. Three families qualify. An English verb may reach its object through a preposition — *hearken unto*, *spake unto*, *inquire of*, *fight against*, *send for* — where that preposition exists only to attach the object to the verb; it is the marker's rendering, not the object noun's, and the marker heads on it. An appositional or resumptive marker may be rendered *even* or *to wit*. **But only a marker standing on the very phrase that English word introduces.** Where the ASV writes an appositional *even* or *to wit* before a phrase no marker marks, no morpheme licenses it and it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, whatever markers stand elsewhere in the clause: `וְחַקּוֹתָ עָלֶיהָ עִיר אֵת־יְרוּשָׁלִָם` → *portray upon it a city,* ***even*** *Jerusalem* gives *even* to the marker, which stands on the appositive itself, while `נָתַתִּי לְךָ אֵת־שְׁנֵי עֲוֺנָם לְמִסְפַּר יָמִים שְׁלֹשׁ־מֵאוֹת וְתִשְׁעִים יוֹם` → *a number of days,* ***even*** *three hundred and ninety days* leaves the *even* `added`, because the clause's one marker stands on `שְׁנֵי עֲוֺנָם`, which the ASV renders bare. Do not reach across the clause for a marker to carry such a word, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and*: the word is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them. And a marker on an object the ASV fronts before its clause and resumes inside it with a pronoun may be rendered *as for*: `וְאֶת־הַיְבוּסִי יוֹשְׁבֵי יְרוּשָׁלִַם לֹא־יָכְלוּ בְנֵי־יְהוּדָה לְהוֹרִישָׁם` → *And* ***as for*** *the Jebusites the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out* gives *as for* to the marker, headed on *as* by rule 24, since the resuming *them* is the suffix's under rule 18 and nothing else answers to the two words. **The same limit governs that third family.** Where the ASV writes *as for* before a fronted phrase no marker stands on, no morpheme licenses the expression and it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, headed on *as*: `וּמַרְאֵיהֶם דְּמוּת אֶחָד לְאַרְבַּעְתָּם` → *And* ***as for*** *their appearance, they four had one likeness* leaves the *as for* `added`, because `מַרְאֵיהֶם` is a bare noun and suffix with no marker and no preposition on it. Do not fold the expression into the fronted noun to avoid the `added`, for the reason just given about a surplus *even*, and do not reach for rule 33: that rule gives a supplied function word to a noun whose own case-function licenses it, and a topicalized nominal's fronting is not such a case-function. Where a morpheme does stand on the fronted phrase it takes the expression, whether that morpheme is a marker as above or a fronting `לְ` — `לָאוֹפַנִּים לָהֶם קוֹרָא` → ***As for*** *the wheels, they were called* gives *As for* to the `לְ` under rule 11. Test by subtraction: drop the English word and ask which morpheme has lost its rendering. If nothing but the object relation is diminished, the marker takes the word; if the ASV writes the object bare — *he built the house* — the marker is `unrepresented`. Do not confuse H853 with its homograph the preposition `אֵת` *with* (H854), which is an ordinary preposition aligning by rule 11.
amendments.why: Rule 16 states its 'only a marker standing on the very phrase' limit for *even* and *to wit*, then introduces the *as for* family afterwards without repeating it. A verse pass reading the rule in order can conclude the limit does not govern *as for*, and EZK.10.10 and EZK.10.22 did exactly that, folding a supplied *as for* onto the fronted noun by analogy to rule 33 while the same chapter marked a supplied appositional *even* `added` in EZK.10.12 for a phrase of identical shape. The amendment closes the gap by naming *as for* in the limit and by saying why the fronted noun is not a candidate, and it records the positive case — a fronting לְ that does stand on the phrase, as in EZK.10.13 — so the rule decides both ways rather than only the negative. This is a correction to the sentence that caused the split rather than a new rule pointing back at it. It is narrow and does not touch the marker's other two families, the subtraction test, or the H853/H854 caution. Evidence: rule 16's own Jebusites example awards *as for* to the marker on the ground that nothing else answers to the two words, which presupposes the fronted noun is not a candidate; the contract's uniform treatment of a surplus supplied word in rules 42, 51 and 55; and the corpus, where all six `as for` units on this lemma sit on a present אֵת and none on a bare nominal. Nothing in the corpus supplied contradicts it. I did not extend the amendment to a preposition taking an appositional *even*, as in EZK.10.2's אֶל: that rests on one hedged occurrence with no corpus support, so it is recorded as a chapter convention instead.

conventions: A supplied *as for* or appositional *even* goes to a morpheme standing on the phrase it introduces, and is `added` where none stands there. In this chapter the fronting לְ of לָאוֹפַנִּים takes *As for* (10:13) and the אֶל standing on *under the cherub* takes *even* (10:2), while the *as for* of 10:10 and 10:22 and the *even* of 10:12 stand before bare nouns carrying no marker and no preposition and are each their own `added` unit. The fronted noun does not take the expression: rule 33 gives a supplied function word to a noun whose own case-function licenses it, and topicalization is not a case-function.

בֵּינוֹת לַ and תַּחַת לַ are split, not fused: בֵּינוֹת and תַּחַת take *between* and *under*, the assimilated article takes the written *the* (rule 12), and the לְ is its own `unrepresented` unit (rule 40) — the shape rule 27 already carves out for the לְ of לֵאמֹר. All six occurrences (10:2 ×3, 10:6 ×2, 10:7) go that way. What fuses under rule 30 here is a compound whose single English word no member's own lexeme supplies: מֵעַל → *from* (10:4, 10:16), בְּתוֹךְ → *within* (10:10), לְעֻמַּת → *beside* and מִלְמָעְלָה → *above* (10:19), כְּעֵין → *like unto* (10:9). Where the ASV spends a word on each member the pair splits instead, as *from over* does in 10:18.

The two occurrences of אוֹתָם are read differently on the ASV's evidence, though MACULA tags both `To`: in 10:17 it is the preposition אֵת *with* (H854), which the ASV renders *with them* after *mounted up*, so the preposition takes *with* under rule 11; in 10:22 it is the object marker H853, whose suffix alone is realized by *themselves* while the marker itself goes `unrepresented` under rule 16.

report: One real split, and it is the kind the candidate table cannot see, because it lives in the `added` units. The chapter answered a single question two ways: when the ASV supplies a discourse function expression (*as for*, appositional *even*) before a phrase carrying no marker and no preposition, who takes it? In 10:12 it marked the *even* before אוֹפַנֵּיהֶם `added` under rule 16. In 10:10 and 10:22 it folded the *as for* onto מַרְאֵיהֶם and דְּמוּת — bare nouns of the same morphological shape, noun plus suffix, with nothing standing on them.

Patched 10:10 and 10:22 so the supplied *as for* is its own `added` unit, which is what rule 16's sentence about a phrase no marker marks requires and what the chapter already did in 10:12. Untouched: 10:13, where a real fronting לְ stands and takes *As for*, and 10:2, where an אֶל stands on the phrase the *even* introduces.

The earlier basis for folding was rule 33 by analogy. It does not reach: rule 33 gives a supplied function word to a noun whose own case-function licenses it (*as a bird*, *to your mountain*), and a topicalized nominal's fronting is not a case-function. Rule 16's Jebusites example points the other way — it awards *as for* to the marker on the ground that nothing else answers to the two words, which it could not say if the fronted noun were itself a candidate.

Cleared as licensed differences rather than splits: מֵעַל fuses to *from* in 10:4 and 10:16 but splits in 10:18, where the ASV writes *from over*, a word for each preposition. כְּעֵין, בְּתוֹךְ, לְעֻמַּת and מִלְמָעְלָה fuse on the same test. בֵּינוֹת לַ / תַּחַת לַ split with the לְ `unrepresented` in all six occurrences; that differs from the fusions because *between* and *under* are בֵּינוֹת's and תַּחַת's own lexemes while the לְ contributes nothing the ASV spends a word on — the shape rule 27 already carves out for לֵאמֹר. Recorded as a convention.

Also checked and consistent, with the source licensing each difference: every unrepresented article answers to an ASV phrase with no *the* (*a wheel*, *one cherub*, *another cherub*, *linen*, and the rule 47 agreement articles of 10:3 and 10:5); every object marker follows rule 16's subtraction test, taking *with* and *of* in 10:4 where the verb reaches its object through a preposition and nothing elsewhere; every supplied object pronoun with no object morpheme is `added` (10:2, 10:7 ×3); every copula sits on the predicate and never on an explicit pronoun subject (10:15, 10:20, 10:22); רָאָה, הלך, אֶחָד, בְּ + infinitive and כִּי all vary only where the ASV's own wording varies.

BSB disagreements: none is a genuine error. The Td × 10 and Rd × 5 blocks are the documented convention difference — BSB attaches an unrendered article or preposition to its phrase where this project leaves it `unrepresented`. The five R items are לֵאמֹר's לְ (rule 27), אַחֲרָיו under the *followed* recasting, 10:13's recast passive לָ, 10:22's compressed אֶל and 10:21's gapped possessive לְ. The 10:3 suffix is anticipatory of the explicit הָאִישׁ, which the ASV renders once; the 10:12 suffix's possession is already carried by *that they four had*; the 10:22 suffix has no possessive written in *straight forward*; the 10:21 numeral is the second member of a distributive doubling. I did not touch any accepted edge to move the 95.0% figure.

10:21's distributive אַרְבָּעָה אַרְבָּעָה gives the single *four* to the first occurrence. Rule 22's tail-to-tail ruling is expressly limited to a counted noun distributed across a compound numeral, so it does not govern a repeated numeral, and neither Hebrew nor English word order distinguishes the two members here. Left as aligned with its competing reading noted, not promoted.
